rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Pteridophytes are seedless vascular plants that represent the evolutionary transition between non-vascular bryophytes and seed-bearing plants. The sporophyte (2n) is the dominant generation; the gametophyte (prothallus) is small and free-living. Ferns like Dryopteris have fronds with sori (spore clusters). Fertilisation still requires water.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Life cycle: Spore (n) → Prothallus (n, gametophyte) → Sperm + Egg → Zygote (2n) → Young sporophyte (2n, dominant) → Sori → Spores (n)
Sori: clusters of sporangia on the underside of fronds
Fertilisation: Sperm (flagellated) + Egg (in archegonium on prothallus) → Zygote (requires water)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Pteridophytes have TRUE vascular tissue (xylem and phloem); bryophytes do NOT. This is the key distinction.  ·  The SPOROPHYTE is the dominant generation in pteridophytes (unlike bryophytes where the gametophyte dominates).

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: NEB expects a detailed diagram of the Dryopteris frond (stipe, blade, pinnae, sori, sporangia, indusium).  ·  The life cycle of a fern (alternation of generations) is a very frequent long-answer question.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Dryopteris filix-medis — common fern, studied for NEB; fronds with sori on the underside.  ·  Equisetum hyemale — horsetail, jointed stem with silica deposits, used in traditional medicine.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: The prothallus (gametophyte) of a fern is small, heart-shaped, and free-living — NOT the main plant body.  ·  Sori are clusters of sporangia on the underside of fern fronds; they are NOT the frond itself.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Pteridophytes: seedless, VASCULAR plants (true xylem + phloem).  ·  Sporophyte (2n) is the dominant, visible generation.  ·  Prothallus (n) is the small, free-living gametophyte.  ·  Reproduction: spores (asexual) + flagellated sperm (sexual, requires water).

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Ferns first appeared in the Carboniferous period (~300 million years ago); their fossils form coal deposits.  ·  The largest fern is the tree fern (Cyathea), which can reach 20 m in height in tropical rainforests.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: Pteridophytes: seedless vascular plants (true xylem and phloem); include ferns, horsetails, clubmosses.  ·  Life cycle: alternation of generations; the sporophyte (2n) is the dominant, visible generation; the gametophyte (n) is small, free-living, and short-lived.  ·  Ferns: frond (leaf-like), rhizome (horizontal stem), stipe (leaf stalk), pinnae; spores in sori on the underside of fronds.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Fern frond: stipe + blade; sori on underside with sporangia.  ·  Economic: medicinal, ornamental, soil, fossil coal deposits.  ·  Fertilisation still requires WATER in pteridophytes (flagellated sperm), even though the sporophyte is dominant.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Pteridophytes do NOT produce seeds; they reproduce by spores. Gymnosperms and angiosperms produce seeds.  ·  Differentiate pteridophytes from bryophytes: key difference is the presence of TRUE vascular tissue and dominant sporophyte.  ·  Note that fertilisation still requires water in pteridophytes — a key exam point.

rows.text: List economic importance of pteridophytes (5 points).  ·  Note that fertilisation requires water even in pteridophytes.  ·  Pteridophytes were the first plants to evolve true vascular tissue.
